---
title: "Fisher information & optimal excitation"
---

## From model to measurement budget

Every measurement experiment faces the same tension: you have a finite amount of
drive power (bounded by actuator saturation) and a finite measurement time (bounded
by how long you can hold an interferometer in a non-standard state).  The question
is not *how much* to drive, but *where*.

The **Fisher information matrix** `I(θ)` is the bridge.
It quantifies, for a given model θ and experimental design (Pxx, T, Pyy),
exactly how many *nats* of information the experiment carries about each parameter
and each pair of parameters.  Its inverse is the Cramér–Rao lower bound — the best
any unbiased estimator can do.

For a single-input / single-output LTI system `G(f; θ)` driven with PSD `Pxx(f)`,
measured in additive noise with PSD `Pyy(f)`, over time `T`:

$$
I_{ij}(\theta) = 2\,T \int_0^{f_s/2}
  \frac{P_{xx}(f)}{P_{yy}(f)}
  \operatorname{Re}\!\left[
    \frac{\partial G^*(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_i}
    \frac{\partial G(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}
  \right] df
$$

(the factor 2 is the circular-complex measurement-noise convention also carried by
the maximum-likelihood fit). `system_ident` exposes this as `fisher.fisher_matrix`
and `fisher.parameter_covariance`; the leading denominator coefficient is held
fixed at 1 (the standard transfer-function gauge), so its row and column are
removed and the matrix is full-rank for any well-excited measurement.

## The dispersion function

Let $M(f)$ be the **marginal Fisher information per unit drive power** at
frequency $f$ — the per-Hz integrand of $I(\theta)$ with the $P_{xx}(f)$ factor
stripped out:

$$
M(f) = \frac{2\,T}{P_{yy}(f)}
  \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\frac{\partial G^*}{\partial \theta}\,
  \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta}\right],
\qquad
I(\theta) = \int P_{xx}(f)\, M(f)\, df .
$$

The **dispersion function** (Pintelon & Schoukens §5.4.2) is the scalar

$$
\nu(f) = P_{\text{tot}} \,\operatorname{tr}\!\left[\, I(\theta)^{-1}\, M(f)\,\right] ,
$$

the sensitivity of the information ellipsoid to a marginal unit of drive power
placed at $f$. High $\nu(f)$ marks the bins where the resonance is strongly
excited *and* the readout noise is not overwhelming the response — exactly where
each extra Hz of drive buys the most parameter information.

By construction the power-weighted average of $\nu$ is the parameter count,
$\int P_{xx}(f)\,\nu(f)\,df / P_{\text{tot}} = \operatorname{tr}[I^{-1}I] = n_\theta$.
The **equivalence theorem** of D-optimal design (Kiefer–Wolfowitz) then says the
information-maximising spectrum is the one for which $\nu(f) = n_\theta$ on the
support of $P_{xx}$ and $\nu(f) \le n_\theta$ elsewhere. Reweighting drive power
toward high-$\nu$ bins under a fixed total-power budget is the Pintelon–Schoukens
fixed-point iteration that flattens $\nu$ to this optimum.

## Interactive comparison

The figure below shows the result for a simple 1 Hz resonance with Q = 20.
The **top panel** is the plant |G(f)|, annotated at the resonance peak.
The **bottom panel** compares the drive ASDs: the optimal allocation
(gold, filled) vs a flat sweep of equal total power (gray, dashed).
Hover over either curve to read exact values; zoom in on the resonance to see
how tightly the optimal drive brackets it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-optimal-excitation
#| fig-cap: "Optimal excitation vs flat drive of equal power, for a 1 Hz / Q=20 resonance. The optimal drive piles power at the resonance; the flat drive spreads it uniformly. Zoom in on 0.8–1.2 Hz to compare."
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

from system_ident.model import TFModel
from system_ident.design.pintelon import optimal_excitation
from system_ident.fisher import parameter_covariance, dispersion

freq   = np.linspace(0.1, 4.0, 600)
model  = TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 20.0)], gain=1.0)
Pyy    = np.ones_like(freq)
Px_tot = 1.0

Pxx_opt  = optimal_excitation(freq, model, Pyy, Px_tot, n_iter=6)
Pxx_flat = np.full_like(freq, Px_tot / (freq[-1] - freq[0]))
resp     = np.abs(model.eval(freq))

T_tot    = 256.0
cov_opt  = parameter_covariance(freq, model, Pxx_opt,  Pyy, T_tot)
cov_flat = parameter_covariance(freq, model, Pxx_flat, Pyy, T_tot)
ratio    = np.max(np.diag(cov_flat)) / np.max(np.diag(cov_opt))

SKY  = '#1F8AC0'
GOLD = '#C8973A'
GRAY = '#94A3B8'

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=2, cols=1,
    shared_xaxes=True,
    subplot_titles=[
        '<b>Plant response</b>  |G(f)|',
        f'<b>Excitation design</b>  — same total power, {ratio:.0f}× variance reduction',
    ],
    vertical_spacing=0.08,
)

# Top: plant response
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=resp,
    mode='lines', line=dict(color=SKY, width=2.5),
    name='|G(f)|',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G| = %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>',
), row=1, col=1)

f0_idx = np.argmax(resp)
fig.add_annotation(
    x=freq[f0_idx], y=resp[f0_idx],
    xref='x', yref='y',
    text='<b>f₀ = 1 Hz, Q = 20</b>',
    showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowsize=1.1,
    arrowcolor='rgba(200,151,58,0.75)',
    ax=60, ay=-35,
    font=dict(size=11, color=GOLD, family='Outfit, sans-serif'),
    row=1, col=1,
)

# Bottom: excitations
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.sqrt(Pxx_opt),
    mode='lines',
    fill='tozeroy', fillcolor='rgba(200,151,58,0.15)',
    line=dict(color=GOLD, width=2.5),
    name='Optimal  (Fisher-matched)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   ASD = %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>',
), row=2, col=1)

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.sqrt(Pxx_flat),
    mode='lines', line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1.8, dash='dash'),
    name='Flat  (equal total power)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   ASD = %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>',
), row=2, col=1)

fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white', height=500,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=50, b=55),
    font=dict(family='Outfit, Inter, sans-serif', size=12),
    legend=dict(
        orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1,
        font=dict(size=11), bgcolor='rgba(255,255,255,0.9)',
        bordercolor='#DCE5F0', borderwidth=1,
    ),
)

fig.update_yaxes(title_text='|G(f)|', type='log', row=1, col=1,
                 gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.update_yaxes(title_text='Drive ASD', row=2, col=1,
                 gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.update_xaxes(title_text='Frequency  [Hz]', row=2, col=1,
                 gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)')
fig.update_xaxes(gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)', row=1, col=1)

fig.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the figure

The optimal drive is **not** centred exactly at f₀ — it is shaped by both the
Jacobian ∂G/∂θ (which peaks near f₀ but is nonzero over a bandwidth set by 1/Q)
and the readout noise PSD Pyy(f).  With flat white noise the result is nearly
Lorentzian, but on real hardware where Pyy rises steeply below ~0.3 Hz,
the optimal drive shifts to higher frequencies where the SNR is better.
:::

## Variance reduction in numbers

```{python}
#| label: tbl-variance
#| echo: false
print(f"{'Excitation':<28} {'Max parameter variance':>24}   {'Relative'}")
print("-" * 65)
print(f"{'Flat (equal power)':<28} {np.max(np.diag(cov_flat)):>24.3e}   1.0 ×")
print(f"{'Optimal (Fisher-matched)':<28} {np.max(np.diag(cov_opt)):>24.3e}   {1/ratio:.4f} ×  ({ratio:.0f}× lower)")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How the iteration converges

`optimal_excitation(freq, model, Pyy, Px_tot, n_iter=3)` runs three rounds of the
fixed-point update.  In practice 3–6 iterations are enough; you can verify
convergence by comparing the output ASD across successive calls.
The API is:

```python
from system_ident.design.pintelon import optimal_excitation

Pxx = optimal_excitation(
    freq,       # frequency array [Hz]
    model,      # TFModel (current prior)
    Pyy,        # readout noise PSD [units²/Hz]
    Px_tot,     # total drive power budget [units²]
    n_iter=3,   # fixed-point iterations
)
```
:::

## What happens at each iteration

Starting from a flat initial guess `Pxx⁽⁰⁾`, each iteration applies the
multiplicative dispersion reweighting of `design.pintelon.optimal_excitation`:

1. Build the Fisher matrix `I(θ; Pxx⁽ᵏ⁾)` and the per-bin information density
   `M(f)` from the current model's Jacobian and the readout noise `Pyy`.
2. Evaluate the dispersion `ν⁽ᵏ⁾(f) = P_tot · tr[I⁻¹ M(f)]` at every bin.
3. Reweight and renormalise:
   `Pxx⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾(f) ∝ Pxx⁽ᵏ⁾(f) · ν⁽ᵏ⁾(f)`, rescaled so `∫ Pxx⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ df = Px_tot`.
   Power flows toward bins with `ν > n_θ` and away from bins with `ν < n_θ`; the
   fixed point is reached when `ν` is flat (`= n_θ`) across the support.
4. Repeat. Two or three iterations usually suffice — pushing further makes the
   design lean too heavily on the (still imperfect) prior model.

After convergence the excitation is synthesised as a **periodic multisine** via
`excitation.multisine_from_psd`: lines placed on the synchronous bin grid at
amplitudes `√(2·Pxx·df)`, with low-crest **Schroeder phases** and a leading Tukey
ramp. Because the waveform is periodic over the analysis window, the response DFT
is leakage-free — see [the method overview](overview.qmd) and the
[worked examples](../examples/01-single-resonance.qmd).

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*,
2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — §5.4.2 (dispersion-function optimal input
design), within the book's Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao framework. The
D-optimal equivalence theorem is due to Kiefer & Wolfowitz (1960).

[LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information
expressions for suspension parameters, the form ported into `fisher.fisher_matrix`.
